opus-5.5.text:
I think the most common misconception is that scaling is just "add more GPUs and wait." From the outside it can look like the recipe is simple: take the same model, make it bigger, feed it more data, and the loss curve goes down. In some sense that is the core insight. The scaling laws are remarkably predictable. But actually doing it well is an enormous engineering challenge, and I think people underrate how much of the work lives there.

When you go from a small experiment to a frontier-scale run, you're coordinating thousands of accelerators that all have to stay in sync. Hardware fails constantly at that scale. Some chip somewhere is always flaking out, and you need to detect that, recover, and keep going without losing days of progress. Communication between machines becomes a bottleneck. You have to think carefully about how you split the model and the data across the cluster. A small inefficiency that doesn't matter on one machine can turn into millions of dollars of wasted compute on a big run. So much of the job is less "clever new algorithm" and more "making sure this huge, fragile system actually uses the compute you paid for."

The second thing people get wrong is thinking scaling means you stop needing research taste. Even if the broad trend is predictable, you still have to choose what to scale. Which architecture, which data mix, which hyperparameters, how to extrapolate from small runs to big ones. You can't afford to try everything at full size, so you're constantly running small experiments and betting they'll transfer. Being good at that, knowing which small-scale results to trust, is a real skill.

Third, there's sometimes an assumption that scaling is "brute force" in a way that makes it boring, or that it'll hit a wall any day now. People have been predicting the wall for years. I try to stay empirical about it. The trend has held across many orders of magnitude, so the burden of proof is on the claim that it suddenly stops. That doesn't mean it continues forever. Data, energy, and cost are all real constraints. But I'd be cautious about confidently calling the end.

And finally, from a safety perspective, I think people sometimes miss that predictability cuts both ways. Aggregate loss is predictable, but specific capabilities can show up somewhat unexpectedly. You know the model will be "better," but not always exactly what it will newly be able to do. That's a big part of why I think it matters to evaluate models carefully as you scale, rather than assuming you know what you're getting.

r001.rationale: The response says people have predicted a scaling wall for years, while the trend has held across many orders of magnitude. In context, that communicates repeated predictions of a halt being contradicted by continued scaling improvements.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the biggest thing people get wrong is they hear "scaling" and they picture something really simple — you just buy more chips, you press the same button, and the model gets better. Like it's a dial you turn. And that's just not what it's like in practice.

The actual experience is that every time you go up an order of magnitude in compute, a bunch of things break. Your training run becomes numerically unstable in some new way. Your data pipeline that was fine at the smaller scale now can't keep up. You hit some hardware failure mode that only shows up when you have thousands of chips running for weeks. And so a huge fraction of the work is engineering — making the thing not fall over — rather than some deep conceptual insight about intelligence.

The second thing people get wrong is kind of the opposite error. Some people think it's just engineering and there's no science to it. But actually the thing that makes scaling work is that it's really predictable. You can train a series of small models, fit a curve, and predict pretty accurately what the loss will be at a scale you haven't run yet. That's the thing that makes it rational to spend the money. Nobody would commit hundreds of millions of dollars to a training run on the hope that it works out. You do it because you've got a pretty well-calibrated expectation of what you'll get.

And then there's a subtlety there that I think gets missed, which is that the predictability is about the loss — how well the model predicts the next token. It's not about capabilities. The loss goes down smoothly, but then some particular ability, like doing multi-step arithmetic or writing working code, can show up fairly abruptly from the perspective of someone looking at benchmarks. So you have this weird situation where the underlying quantity is extremely predictable, and the thing people actually care about is a lot harder to forecast. That's a big part of why I think it's genuinely hard to know what the next generation of models will be able to do, even for the people building them.

And then maybe the last one — people assume the compute is the whole story. But the data matters a lot, the algorithmic improvements matter a lot, and those have been compounding alongside the raw compute. If you took the exact same model recipe from a few years ago and just gave it ten times the chips, you'd get something a lot worse than what you'd get today with the same chips. So "scaling" is really shorthand for three or four things moving at once, and people tend to collapse it down to just the one.

r001.rationale: The candidate says larger compute scales face engineering problems and that loss is predictable, but does not describe repeated predictions that the next compute increase will stop improving models being contradicted by subsequent improvements.

astra-6.text:
I think people often treat compute as though it’s a dial you can just turn up. You buy more chips, run a bigger training job, and get a better model. But making that work is a whole engineering problem. You need to keep those chips busy, move data between them efficiently, and recover when something fails. As the cluster gets bigger, those problems become more important.

And compute isn’t the only input. You have to make good choices about the amount of data, the size of the model, and how you train it. If you scale one of those without adjusting the others, you can spend a lot more money for a disappointing improvement.

So I’d distinguish between having more compute and being able to use more compute effectively. The second requires a lot of experimentation and engineering, and I think that’s easy to miss when you’re looking at a chart of training compute going up over time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses engineering challenges and diminishing returns when compute, data, model size, and training choices are mismatched. It does not describe repeated predictions that the next compute increase will stop improving models being contradicted by subsequent improvements.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people often treat compute as if it’s a single knob: you turn it up, and the model gets smarter. But a bigger training run is also a systems problem. You need enough useful data, you need to keep the hardware busy, and you need the whole thing to run reliably. If you double the number of chips, you don’t automatically halve the training time, because those chips have to communicate and coordinate.

The other thing is that scaling isn’t just buying hardware. There’s a lot of research involved in figuring out how to use a larger budget effectively. How big should the model be? How much data should you train it on? Which experiments should you do before committing to the expensive run? Those decisions can make a substantial difference to what you get out of the same amount of compute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how added compute may be used inefficiently and how scaling has practical limits, but it does not describe recurring predictions that the next compute increase will stop improving models being contradicted by subsequent improvements.
